evidence:
Premise 1, C# 15 introduces labeled break and continue and the label is an ordinary labeled statement. Confirmed. The proposal at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dotnet/csharplang/main/proposals/csharp-15.0/labeled-break-continue.md gives the grammar "break_statement : 'break' identifier? ';'" and "continue_statement : 'continue' identifier? ';'", and specifies the target through an insertion into standard section 13.5 "Labeled statements": "If the statement immediately nested within a labeled_statement is a switch_statement or an iteration_statement, the nested statement is said to be labeled with the identifier of the labeled_statement." The proposal's own example is "outer: for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < 10; j++) { if (i * j > 20) break outer; } }". The same shape is recorded at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Metalama/ccf204f4-b0b3-5fe6-a8de-fe20f6791d2c/scratchpad/impact/08-roslyn-api-delta.md:126. The feature is part of C# 15: FACTS.md:31 records that MessageID.IDS_FeatureLabeledBreakContinue requires LanguageVersion.CSharp15 on Roslyn main.

Premise 2, the label of a labeled loop lives in the ordinary label declaration space, so two identical labels are a compile-time error. Confirmed, and the proposal changes nothing here. The proposal quotes the standard verbatim in its "Open questions" section: "Each block or switch_block creates a separate declaration space for labels. ... The label declaration space of a block includes any nested blocks. Thus, within a nested block it is not possible to declare a label with the same name as a label in an enclosing block." and "The scope of a label is the whole block in which the label is declared, including any nested blocks. It is a compile-time error for two labels with the same name to have overlapping scopes." The diff sections of the proposal touch only 13.5 (adding the "labeled with" paragraph), 13.10.2 and 13.10.3; they do not touch the declaration-space or shadowing rules.

Premise 3, the diagnostics are CS0140 in one block and CS0158 across nested blocks. Confirmed against dotnet/roslyn main. src/Compilers/CSharp/Portable/Errors/ErrorCode.cs line 118 "ERR_DuplicateLabel = 140" and line 136 "ERR_LabelShadow = 158". src/Compilers/CSharp/Portable/CSharpResources.resx gives the texts "The label '{0}' is a duplicate" and "The label '{0}' shadows another label by the same name in a contained scope". Both are reported from BindLabeledStatement in src/Compilers/CSharp/Portable/Binder/Binder_Statements.cs, ERR_DuplicateLabel at line 486 when the looked-up label symbol is not the one being declared, and ERR_LabelShadow at line 498 after a lookup in binder.Next, that is in the enclosing scopes. Both are errors, not warnings, and both are reported on the labeled statement itself, independently of any break or continue that references it. The linker's flattened and non-flattened cases therefore both end in a compile-time error, as the finding states.

Premise 4, the label of a labeled loop is resolved by name at binding time and an unresolvable name is an error. Confirmed. Binder_Statements.cs lines 2956-2991 (BindBreakOrContinue) calls MessageID.IDS_FeatureLabeledBreakContinue.CheckFeatureAvailability, resolves the target with GetBreakLabel(labelName) or GetContinueLabel(labelName), and reports ERR_NoBreakId or ERR_NoContinueId when the target is null. The delta report records these as CS9393 and CS9394 (08-roslyn-api-delta.md:129), and ErrorCode.cs lines 2505-2506 confirm the numbers.

Premise 5, BreakStatementSyntax.Name and ContinueStatementSyntax.Name do not exist in Roslyn 5.0.0, and SyntaxFactory.BreakStatement(attributeLists, breakKeyword, name, semicolonToken) exists in the newer API. Confirmed. 08-roslyn-api-delta.md:66-68 lists Name, WithName and the four-parameter Update on both statements, and the three new SyntaxFactory overloads, as new members first present in the 5.10 window, absent from 5.0. FACTS.md:26 records the same field as a new optional experimental field on both nodes in eng/src/GenerateMetaSyntaxRewriter/Syntax-5.10.0.xml.

Premise 6, no new SyntaxKind is involved, so the collection of LabeledStatementSyntax nodes proposed by the finding is unaffected. Confirmed: 08-roslyn-api-delta.md:99, "No SyntaxKind for a labeled break; SyntaxKind.LabeledStatement (8799) is reused for the target label."

Premise 7, a generic rewriter over IdentifierNameSyntax needs no new API. Confirmed as far as the external surface goes: the Name is an IdentifierNameSyntax child node of the break or continue statement (08-roslyn-api-delta.md:66 and the proposal's grammar), so it is reached by the ordinary child traversal of CSharpSyntaxRewriter, and testing node.Parent.IsKind(SyntaxKind.BreakStatement) uses only SyntaxKind values that already exist in 5.0.

Corrections found. (a) The finding names "the 5.10 variant" as the place for the strongly typed rewrite. FACTS.md:48-49 (the addendum, which supersedes the reports) states that no stable 5.10, 5.11 or 5.12 package exists on nuget.org, that dotnet/roslyn main is versioned 5.12, and that the November 2026 baseline is expected to carry Roslyn 5.12, the transition being a renumbering of the latest variant to 5.12.0. The correct wording is "the latest Roslyn variant", expected to be Roslyn.5.12.0. (b) In the build Metalama consumes today, and in stable 5.9.0, the Name members are marked [RSEXPERIMENTAL006] and the Syntax.xml field carries ExperimentalUrl (08-roslyn-api-delta.md:66-67 and the "Attribute changes" paragraph at line 90; FACTS.md:26-27). The markers were removed by the commit "Add C# 15 language version (#84799)" of 2026-08-11 (08-roslyn-api-delta.md:17). A strongly typed use of Name against the consumed preview therefore needs an RSEXPERIMENTAL006 suppression, which the generic IdentifierNameSyntax rewrite avoids; against a 5.12 build no suppression is needed. (c) The finding's claim that the collision cannot occur today is a plausibility statement, not an impossibility: a label with no reference is legal C#, reported only by the warning WRN_UnreferencedLabel, that is CS0164, "This label has not been referenced" (ErrorCode.cs line 142 and CSharpResources.resx). A user could write a useless label in a template today and reach the same CS0140 or CS0158. (d) The scenario is gated on work not yet done: FACTS.md:54 records that LanguageVersion.CSharp15 is absent from 5.9.0 and from the consumed 5.10 preview, so labeled break and continue are reachable there only under LanguageVersion.Preview, and FACTS.md:16 and FACTS.md:22 record that Metalama caps the language version at C# 14 and rewrites an implied LangVersion of 15.0 to 12.0.

Additional external fact relevant to the proposed change, not contradicting the finding. The parser accepts the name unconditionally, with no language-version test: src/Compilers/CSharp/Portable/Parser/LanguageParser.cs lines 9354-9370, ParseBreakStatement and ParseContinueStatement pass "this.IsTrueIdentifier() ? this.ParseIdentifierName() : null" to the factory, and the version check is performed later at binding (Binder_Statements.cs line 2966). A BreakStatementSyntax with a non-null Name can therefore reach Metalama from any compilation parsed by such a Roslyn, whatever the effective language version. Combined with the "immediately nested" rule quoted above and its note ("Only the statement that is immediately nested within a labeled_statement is labeled with that identifier"), two further failure modes follow from the language rules: a rewrite that drops the Name turns "break outer;" into "break;", which exits the inner loop instead of the outer one with no diagnostic at all; and a rewrite that inserts any statement or block between the label and the loop makes the label no longer label the loop, so every "break outer;" inside it fails with CS9393 or CS9394.

corrections.what_happens_today: Before C# 15 a label is reachable only from a goto statement, and templates cannot use goto, so a label in a template body is legal but useless. It is not impossible today: an unreferenced label is reported only by the warning CS0164 ("This label has not been referenced"), so a template carrying a dead label and a target method carrying a label of the same name already collide. The case becomes realistic with C# 15, because labeled break and continue make `outer: foreach (...) { ... break outer; }` an ordinary idiom (csharplang proposal csharp-15.0/labeled-break-continue.md). A template that contains such a loop and is inlined into a target method that also declares `outer` yields two `outer:` labels in one block after flattening, which is CS0140 ERR_DuplicateLabel, "The label '{0}' is a duplicate", or, when the blocks are not flattened, CS0158 ERR_LabelShadow, "The label '{0}' shadows another label by the same name in a contained scope". Both are errors, reported on the labeled statement itself and independently of any break or continue that references it (dotnet/roslyn main, Binder_Statements.cs lines 486 and 498). The proposal changes neither the label declaration space nor the shadowing rule; it quotes both unchanged. The scenario is gated on C# 15 actually being enabled in Metalama: the consumed Roslyn build has no LanguageVersion.CSharp15, and Metalama currently caps the language version at C# 14 and rewrites an implied LangVersion of 15.0 to 12.0 (FACTS.md:16, 22, 54).
corrections.proposed_change: Add a label-renaming substitution applied to inlined bodies: collect LabeledStatementSyntax identifiers of the inlined body, allocate unique names through LexicalScopeFactory.GetLexicalScope( destination ).GetUniqueIdentifier, and rewrite LabeledStatementSyntax.Identifier, GotoStatementSyntax.Expression, and the Name of BreakStatementSyntax and ContinueStatementSyntax. The last two members do not exist in Roslyn 5.0.0, and in the build consumed today they are marked [RSEXPERIMENTAL006]; the marker was removed by the Roslyn commit "Add C# 15 language version (#84799)" of 2026-08-11. A strongly typed rewrite, rebuilding the statement with SyntaxFactory.BreakStatement( attributeLists, breakKeyword, name, semicolonToken ), therefore belongs in the latest Roslyn variant only, which the addendum expects to be renumbered Roslyn.5.12.0 rather than 5.10.0, and needs an RSEXPERIMENTAL006 suppression until that variant is built from a Roslyn later than 2026-08-11. The alternative that works in both variants without a suppression is a CSharpSyntaxRewriter override of VisitIdentifierName that tests whether the parent node is a BreakStatement or a ContinueStatement; it uses only SyntaxKind values that already exist in Roslyn 5.0. Two language rules must also be respected by whatever rewrites these statements. First, only the statement immediately nested within a labeled statement is labeled with that identifier (proposal, note on standard section 13.5), so the rewrite must not insert a statement or a block between a label and the loop it labels, on pain of CS9393 ERR_NoBreakId or CS9394 ERR_NoContinueId. Second, dropping the Name of a break or continue statement produces no diagnostic at all and silently retargets the jump to the innermost loop, so any rewriter that rebuilds these statements must preserve the Name. Add linker tests Methods/Overrides/Labels/* with a labeled loop in both the override and the target.
corrections.consequence_class: Build or restore error (in the transformed compilation). The label collision is CS0140 or CS0158. Two adjacent failure modes of the same rewrite are CS9393 or CS9394 (a label that no longer labels the loop) and, if the Name of a break or continue statement is dropped, a silent change of control flow with no diagnostic.

notes:
Every external premise of the finding is true. The C# 15 feature exists, the label it uses is an ordinary labeled statement, the label declaration space and the shadowing rule are unchanged by the proposal, and the two diagnostics the finding names are the correct ones, both errors, both reported on the label declaration rather than on the break statement. The Roslyn API premises are also correct: Name is new after 5.0, the four-parameter SyntaxFactory overload exists, and no new SyntaxKind is involved.

Three corrections were applied, none of which the finding depends on. The variant that can use the strongly typed API is the latest variant, which the FACTS addendum expects to be renumbered 5.12.0, not 5.10.0. That API is still marked [RSEXPERIMENTAL006] in the build consumed today, so the generic rewrite over IdentifierNameSyntax that the finding already offers as an alternative is the one that compiles in both variants without a suppression. And the "cannot happen today" framing is a plausibility argument rather than an impossibility, because an unreferenced label is only a warning.

I did not manage to refute the collision mechanism from the language side. The one avenue that could have refuted it, a separate declaration space or a relaxed uniqueness rule for loop labels, is explicitly closed by the proposal, which quotes the existing declaration-space and overlapping-scope rules without modifying them and only adds the "labeled with" paragraph.

Two facts found during verification extend the finding rather than contradict it, and both are recorded in the corrections. The parser accepts the label name with no language-version test (LanguageParser.cs lines 9354-9370), so the node can reach Metalama regardless of the effective language version, and the version check happens at binding. And because only the statement immediately nested within the labeled statement is labeled with the identifier, a rewrite that separates the label from its loop, or that drops the Name of a break or continue statement, fails in ways that are not label collisions: CS9393 or CS9394 in the first case, and a silent retargeting of the jump to the innermost loop in the second.

The finding's open question about whether the template compiler preserves BreakStatementSyntax.Name is not resolved here, because it is a code question. The external half of it is settled: the field carries ExperimentalUrl in Syntax-5.10.0.xml, and the generator strips such fields (FACTS.md:26-27), so no generated visitor knows about it today, and that changes when the latest variant moves to a Roslyn later than 2026-08-11.

corrections.what_happens_today: The scenario requires a compilation that contains a union. LanguageVersion.CSharp15 does not exist in the consumed Roslyn build, so a union is only parsed under LanguageVersion.Preview, which the compile-time pipeline accepts only when AllowPreviewLanguageFeatures is set (Pipeline/CompileTime/CompileTimeAspectPipeline.cs:70-80). With that option set, the advice code runs to completion today and only the emission fails, in the manner described by LK-1. After LK-1 and LK-2 are fixed, four distinct outcomes follow. First, AddInitializer(BeforeInstanceConstructor) enumerates every constructor of the union. The synthesized one-parameter case constructors are implicitly declared but have a non-empty parameter list, so IsImplicitInstanceConstructor is false and the statements are attached to a constructor that has no syntax; the linker stores them in a dictionary keyed by that constructor and no visitor ever consumes them, so they are silently lost. No assertion fires. Second, the same enumeration also reaches the implicit parameterless constructor that Roslyn synthesizes for every struct, including a union; that one satisfies IsImplicitInstanceConstructor, so a ConstructorBuilder materializes an explicit parameterless constructor, and the compiler rejects it with ERR_UnionConstructorCallsDefaultConstructor, 'A constructor declared in a union declaration must have a this initializer that calls a synthesized constructor or an explicitly declared constructor.' Third, AddInitializer(AfterLastInstanceConstructor) goes through OnConstructedEpilogueEmitter, which does not emit forwarding constructors: it introduces an InitializationContext parameter that carries default(InitializationContext) and creates the pull implementation without a forwarding helper. On a union it materializes the implicit parameterless constructor and appends that parameter to it, producing an explicitly declared public constructor with a single parameter, which the compiler rejects with ERR_InstanceCtorWithOneParameterInUnion in addition to ERR_UnionConstructorCallsDefaultConstructor; the parameter introductions targeting the syntax-less case constructors are silently lost. The forwarding constructor with the pre-mutation single-parameter signature comes instead from the required-parameter IntroduceParameter overload, whose default overloading strategy is ForwardSourceConstructors: applied to a case constructor it emits a public constructor with that one parameter, which the compiler rejects for the same reason and which also duplicates the signature of the synthesized case constructor. Fourth, IntroduceField, automatic property and field-like event introductions, and an interface implementation whose member template is an automatic property or a field-like event, emit an instance field, which the compiler rejects with ERR_InstanceFieldInUnion, 'Instance fields, auto-properties or field-like events are not permitted in a union declaration.' The helper that the interface path also calls, OverrideHelper.AddTransformationsForStructField, does not introduce the backing field: it materializes the first implicitly declared constructor of the struct as an explicit parameterless constructor, which on a union adds ERR_UnionConstructorCallsDefaultConstructor.
corrections.consequence_class: Build or restore error, because the transformed compilation fails on generated code with ERR_InstanceFieldInUnion (CS9373), ERR_InstanceCtorWithOneParameterInUnion (CS9374) and ERR_UnionConstructorCallsDefaultConstructor (CS9375). In addition, silent wrong output for the statements and parameters that target the synthesized one-parameter case constructors, which are dropped without any diagnostic and without any assertion.
corrections.proposed_change: The route through the per-advice-kind eligibility rules does not work as stated, for three reasons. The rules are shared objects: _introduceRule is the rule for IntroduceMethod, IntroduceFinalizer, IntroduceOperator, IntroduceField, IntroduceEvent, IntroduceProperty, IntroduceIndexer and IntroduceConstructor alike, so a rule cannot be added for IntroduceField alone without splitting it. The rules see only the target type, so they cannot distinguish an automatic property from a template property, nor a field-like event from an accessor event; both map to the same advice kind. And introducing a method, a static field or a nested type into a union is valid C#, so a rule on the target type over-restricts. AdviceFactory.Validate does not report a diagnostic either: it throws an InvalidOperationException carrying the ineligibility justification. Two implementable options remain. The conservative option, small in size, is a blanket check on the target type: add MustNotBeUnion() to _introduceRule, to both branches of _addInitializerRule (the type branch and, through DeclaringType(), the constructor branch), to _introduceParameterRule through DeclaringType(), and to _implementInterfaceRule, so that 2027.0 fails early with the existing eligibility exception and a clear message instead of failing at the linker or in the transformed compilation. The precise option, larger in size, keeps the legal cases working and moves the check into the advice implementations that actually emit an instance field or a constructor: IntroduceFieldAdvice, IntroducePropertyAdvice for the automatic-property shape, IntroduceEventAdvice for the field-like shape, ImplementInterfaceAdvice at the two AddTransformationsForStructField call sites, OverrideHelper.AddTransformationsForStructField itself, ConstructorInitializeAdvice, OnConstructedEpilogueEmitter and the constructor materialization inside IntroduceConstructorParameterAdvice, each reporting a dedicated LAMA diagnostic. Either option depends on a code-model predicate for unions. ITypeSymbol.IsUnion exists only in the latest Roslyn variant and is marked experimental there, and it is absent from the Roslyn 5.0.0 variant, while the eligibility rules live in Metalama.Framework, which has no Roslyn variant; the predicate must therefore be an INamedType member whose implementation lives in the variant-compiled engine and returns false in the 5.0.0 variant.
corrections.size: S for the blanket eligibility check on the target type; L for the precise per-advice validation, because it requires a variant-gated code-model predicate, changes in eight advice implementations, new diagnostics and tests.

notes: The central claim survives: advice is admitted on a union because the code model reports it as a struct, and once the linker can inject into a union declaration the generated code is rejected by the compiler. Three supporting details are wrong and are corrected above. First, OnConstructedEpilogueEmitter does not emit forwarding constructors; it introduces an optional parameter and creates the pull implementation with no forwarding helper. The single-parameter public constructor it produces on a union comes from materializing the implicit parameterless struct constructor and then appending the InitializationContext parameter to it. Forwarding constructors come only from the required-parameter IntroduceParameter overload. Second, OverrideHelper.AddTransformationsForStructField does not introduce backing fields; it materializes the first implicitly declared constructor of a struct. The backing field comes from the introduced automatic property itself. Third, the alternative "or the transformation collection asserts" is not supported by the code; the initializer path loses the statements silently. One compiler error is missing from the finding: ERR_UnionConstructorCallsDefaultConstructor, which fires for every explicit constructor that Metalama materializes or introduces into a union without a this(...) initializer, and which is the most frequent of the three because the implicit parameterless struct constructor is materialized on several paths. The proposed change is the weakest part: the eligibility rules are shared per advice kind and cannot express the restriction, AdviceFactory.Validate throws rather than reports, and a blanket rule over-restricts advice that is legal on a union. Assumptions that remain: the Roslyn sources inspected are the July 2026 main lineage in the scratchpad, and the stable Roslyn 5.12 named in the FACTS addendum is assumed to keep the same union symbol shape, the same three error codes and the same message texts. The verdict is based on reading only; nothing was built and no test was run.

corrections.what_happens_today: Two premises need correction; the mechanism of the finding survives both. First, the implied language version is not produced by the .NET SDK. It is produced by the compiler package's Microsoft.CSharp.Core.targets, which Metalama.Compiler ships as a fork and which the package makes the imported one by setting CSharpCoreTargetsPath (Metalama.Compiler.props:122). The fork keeps the upstream formula (C# version = 9 + target framework major - 5, so net11.0 gives 15.0) and adds only the LangVersionImplicitlySet flag (fork Microsoft.CSharp.Core.targets:34). The open question of the finding is therefore answered: net11.0 is marked, and the marked value is the upstream formula capped at _MaxAvailableLangVersion. Second, the computed value is capped. Metalama.Compiler develop/2027.0 tracks Roslyn 5.10 and caps at 14.0 (fork targets:27), so today a net11.0 project without LangVersion receives LangVersion=14.0 with LangVersionImplicitlySet=True; 14.0 is in the whitelist at Metalama.Framework.targets:118, so no rewrite and no warning occur, and the project compiles as C# 14. The rewrite to 12.0 and the misleading warning described by the finding arise as soon as Metalama.Compiler is rebased on Roslyn 5.12, whose Microsoft.CSharp.Core.targets:27 caps at 15.0 (commit dotnet/roslyn#84799 of 2026-08-11): the implied value then becomes 15.0, which is not in the whitelist. Scenario (b), an explicit 15.0, is accurate for a 5.12 compiler; with the current 5.10 compiler the value is rejected by the command-line parser (CS1617), because LanguageVersion.CSharp15 does not exist in that build (FACTS addendum).
corrections.consequence_class: Unchanged in kind, but conditional in time: the build error on C# 13, 14 or 15 syntax and the uncoded, misleading warning appear exactly with the move of Metalama.Compiler to Roslyn 5.12 that 2027.0 plans, so the targets fix must ship in the same release as that move. With the current compiler the defect is latent.
corrections.proposed_change: The proposed comparison is sound and is simplified by the corrected premise: when LangVersionImplicitlySet is true, LangVersion is always a numeric string produced by the upstream formula (7.3, 8.0 or N.0), never a named value, so VersionLessThan('$(LangVersion)', '12.0') can be applied without a guard for named values; the named entries in the current whitelist are unreachable on that path. The new standalone scenario DefaultLanguageVersion/DotNet11 (net11.0, empty LangVersion, C# 14 feature) is a valid regression guard, but it passes with the current 5.10 compiler (implied 14.0, no rewrite) and fails only once Metalama.Compiler caps at 15.0; the analysis should state that the scenario is a guard for the 5.12 transition rather than a demonstration of a present failure.
corrections.size: Unchanged: S for the targets, M including the container change of LV-9.

corrections.what_happens_today: Metalama.Framework.Engine is compiled once per Roslyn variant from one shared source glob, and Roslyn 5.0 has neither UnionDeclarationSyntax, SyntaxKind.UnionDeclaration, SyntaxKind.UnionKeyword, SyntaxKind.ClosedKeyword, ITypeSymbol.IsUnion, ITypeSymbol.UnionCaseTypes, ITypeSymbol.IsClosed nor ITypeSymbol.GetClosedDerivedTypeInfo. Any of CM-1 to CM-9 that names them fails to compile in the Roslyn.5.0.0 variant. The Roslyn.5.0.0 variant serves Rider and the C# Dev Kit, whose compiler cannot produce a union or a closed class, so the members are needed only in the Roslyn.5.10.0 variant. Two further constraints apply to that variant. First, the Roslyn build consumed by the latest variant does not expose ITypeSymbol.UnionCaseTypes at all: that property is present only from Roslyn 5.11 and on main, so a shim cannot read it publicly from either variant until the move to the stable Roslyn. Second, every union and closed member that the 5.10 surface does expose carries ExperimentalAttribute with the identifier RSEXPERIMENTAL006, which the C# compiler reports as an error by default; the repository has no suppression for it, and its own code generator strips experimental declarations from the grammar for exactly this reason. Naming those members therefore fails to compile in the Roslyn.5.10.0 variant as well, unless the diagnostic is suppressed.
corrections.consequence_class: Compile error of the Metalama.Framework.Engine.5.0.0 variant project (and of the other .5.0.0 variant projects that share their source) for every implementation of the findings above, plus a compile error of the latest variant with the identifier RSEXPERIMENTAL006 wherever an experimental member is named without a suppression. The failure is loud at build time; nothing is silent and nothing crashes at run time. No restore step is involved.
corrections.proposed_change: Decide once, for all themes, between four mechanisms, and note that only the last of them avoids the RSEXPERIMENTAL006 error on the latest variant. (1) `#if ROSLYN_5_10_0_OR_GREATER` blocks, which requires lifting the policy stated in the two .props files and restated in testing.md:58, updating-roslyn.md:36 and extensibility.md:116, and which additionally requires suppressing RSEXPERIMENTAL006 in the guarded region until the union and closed API loses its experimental marker in the stable Roslyn. (2) Numeric kind values ((SyntaxKind) 9082 for UnionDeclaration, 8452 for UnionKeyword, 8453 for ClosedKeyword) with a RoslynApiVersion guard. corrections.what_happens_today: The suppressor locates the declaring member of each reported diagnostic with FindSymbolDeclaringNode, whose kind list names class, struct, interface, record, record struct, enum and delegate but not union (nor extension block, which is already omitted today). A union declaration carries its identifier, its modifiers and its case types on the union node itself: the case types are parsed into the parameter list of UnionDeclarationSyntax, so a diagnostic located on any of them has no member declaration ancestor below the union node. The upward walk therefore passes over the union node. When the union is declared inside a namespace declaration the walk stops at the namespace, and the loop at lines 202 to 215 then resolves symbols from the namespace upwards; when the union is nested in a type the walk stops at the enclosing type; when the union is declared at file scope with no namespace declaration the walk returns null and line 194 skips the diagnostic. In all three cases a suppression registered on the union type is never matched, and the failure is silent, because no assertion and no diagnostic is produced and the serializable identifier of a namespace symbol is computed without error. Diagnostics located inside a member of the union still match, because the member is found and the walk up from it reaches the union node, on which GetDeclaredSymbol succeeds through the BaseTypeDeclarationSyntax case of the general overload. The same helper is used by ScopedSuppression.Matches, so the compile-time suppression path has the same gap. FindMemberDeclaration (called by CodeModelExtensions.ToInsertPosition) and GetDeclaringType (called by LexicalScopeFactory) have the same omission, and their failure mode is not silent: FindMemberDeclaration throws AssertionFailedException when the walk finds nothing, and both call sites in LexicalScopeFactory apply AssertNotNull to the result of GetDeclaringType.

Second, the description covered only the namespace case; the nested case and the file-scope case reach the same outcome by different routes, and the file-scope case exits at line 194 rather than at the loop. On the other hand, the type tests widen the match to enum members and to extension blocks, which the present kind lists exclude, so the change is minimal in size but not strictly behaviour preserving for FindMemberDeclaration and GetDeclaringType; the size estimate of S remains correct.

The finding survives. Every external premise holds: a union is a TypeDeclarationSyntax with its own member list, it has no primary constructor and no positional properties, and the record and class rewrite logic therefore does not apply to it. Two points that strengthen the proposed change rather than weaken it. The union node is experimental in every Roslyn version Metalama consumes today and absent from the Roslyn 5.0 variant, so the kind-based fallback over TypeDeclarationSyntax is the only technique that compiles across the shipped variants; an override of VisitUnionDeclaration is not available. And Roslyn itself separates the union parameter list from a primary constructor by node type, not by the presence of the list, which is the same discipline the fallback needs.

One point that widens the work beyond the finding: the union member restrictions of the proposal, enforced by CS9373, CS9374 and CS9375, mean that fixing the linker dispatch does not by itself make aspects on unions produce compilable output. This belongs to eligibility rather than to linking, so it does not change the size of LK-2, but it should be stated so that the linking fix is not mistaken for complete support.

notes:
The finding survives as an item and its Premium-side conclusion ("None in Premium") is unchanged, but two of its external premises are wrong and its consequence class must change from "No impact" to "no impact in Premium, one silent false negative in the core".

The most consequential correction is the union case-type reference. The finding assumed the reference would be recorded with the union type as its origin, possibly under an unwanted reference kind; in reality the origin cannot be resolved, because Roslyn deliberately gives a union declaration no primary constructor and therefore no declared symbol for the case-type parameters, and Metalama's index drops any reference whose referencing symbol is null. The result is not a mislabelled reference but no reference at all. This is core work, not Premium work, and it is invisible without a test, which makes the proposed aspect test valuable rather than optional.

The second correction concerns the closed class. The compiler rule bans only direct derivation, and it is a module rule rather than an assembly rule. The persisted transitive validator therefore continues to do real work for a closed class, so the sentence claiming redundancy should be removed rather than softened.

Two premises that the finding left open are now settled and should be removed from the open questions: a union symbol has TypeKind.Struct, and the union case-type syntax is a ParameterSyntax with a missing identifier. The remaining open question, whether a dedicated ReferenceKinds member for a union case is wanted, becomes more pointed given refuted premise B: the fix for the missing origin is the natural place to decide whether the case-type reference should be reported as ParameterType or under a new kind.

Finally, the version wording should be corrected everywhere it appears in this finding: there is no stable Roslyn 5.10, the target of the 2027.0 baseline is Roslyn 5.12, and the union API was in fact readable in the stable 5.9.0 assemblies, so the "plausible" confidence rested on a mistaken premise about what could not be inspected.

External premise 3, that the tools reach the .NET 11 runtime through `RollForward=Major`, refuted as stated. The roll-forward table of dotnet/docs, includes/roll-forward-table.md, defines `Major` as "Roll-forward to the next available higher major version ... if requested major version is missing. If the requested major version is present, then the Minor policy is used", and the worked example in docs/core/versions/selection.md:172-180 resolves `Major` to 8.2.3 rather than to 9.7.8 when both are installed. A net10.0 application with `RollForward=Major` therefore runs on .NET 10 whenever a .NET 10 runtime is installed, and reaches .NET 11 only when no .NET 10 runtime is present.

External premise 4, the inference that the simulator process running on .NET 10 prevents a net11.0 project, not supported by the runtime major alone. Roslyn evaluates projects in a separate build host process. At commit 35d9211b, the commit from which the stable 5.9.0 was built and the same lineage as the consumed 5.10.0-1.26365.3 (FACTS.md addendum line 53), src/Workspaces/MSBuild/Core/MSBuild/BuildHostProcessManager.cs:249-252 launches the .NET Core build host with `--roll-forward LatestMajor` and `DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD_TO_PRERELEASE=1`, and line 155 calls `FindBestMSBuildAsync(projectOrSolutionFilePath)` and then relaunches the build host from the `dotnet` executable that belongs to the selected MSBuild (main, lines 148-175). The shipped runtimeconfig confirms the roll-forward: `contentFiles/any/any/BuildHost-netcore/Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspaces.MSBuild.BuildHost.runtimeconfig.json` in the 5.9.0 package declares `"tfm": "net8.0"` and `"rollForward": "Major"`. The interaction with the in-process registration is not settled from outside the code: microsoft/MSBuildLocator src/MSBuildLocator/MSBuildLocator.cs:331-344 shows that registering a .NET SDK instance sets `MSBUILD_EXE_PATH`, `MSBuildExtensionsPath` and `MSBuildSDKsPath` in the current process, and a child process inherits them.

External premise 5, the fact that does support the conclusion, confirmed. The .NET SDK rejects a target framework above its own bundled one: dotnet/sdk src/Layout/redist/targets/GenerateBundledVersions.targets:714 sets `<NETCoreAppMaximumVersion>$(_NETCoreAppTargetFrameworkVersion)</NETCoreAppMaximumVersion>`, that is the SDK's own bundled .NETCoreApp version, and Microsoft.NET.TargetFrameworkInference.targets:192-198 raises `UnsupportedTargetFrameworkVersion` when `_TargetFrameworkVersionWithoutV` exceeds it, from a target whose `BeforeTargets` includes `Restore` and `CollectPackageReferences`. A net11.0 project therefore fails under the pinned .NET 10 SDK at restore, which is the step that DesignTimeSolution.cs:60-68 performs.

corrections.what_happens_today:
eng/src/DesignTimeSolution.cs:42 sets `_simulatorTargetFramework` to "net10.0" and Metalama.DesignTime.HostSimulator.csproj:6 targets net10.0. MSBuildEnvironment.cs:50 selects the highest installed .NET SDK whose major version does not exceed `Environment.Version.Major`, and MSBuildInitializer.cs:84 applies the same rule. Metalama.Framework.Workspaces.csproj:18 targets net10.0 because Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspaces.MSBuild ships assets for net10.0 and net472 only. That statement holds for the stable 5.9.0 package and for the consumed prerelease 5.10.0-1.26365.3, and it will still hold for the expected November 2026 stable, because dotnet/roslyn main sets NetRoslyn and NetRoslynAll to net10.0 and the project targets `$(NetRoslynSourceBuild);net472`. There is no stable Microsoft.CodeAnalysis package numbered 5.10, and the stable that the 2027.0 baseline is expected to consume is 5.12. Raising RoslynMaxVersion therefore does not by itself allow the workspaces project to move to net11.0.

No design-time scenario can contain a net11.0 project today, but the decisive reason is the .NET SDK pinned for the build rather than the runtime of the simulator process. eng/src/Program.cs:26 pins the SDK at 10.0.400, and the .NET SDK raises the UnsupportedTargetFrameworkVersion error for any target framework above its own bundled version, from a target that runs before Restore, so the restore that DesignTimeSolution.cs:60-68 performs fails on a net11.0 project. The runtime of the simulator process is a second constraint of a narrower kind: the MSBuild of the .NET 11 SDK targets net11.0, so it cannot be loaded into a process running on the .NET 10 runtime, and the selection rule at MSBuildEnvironment.cs:50 excludes the .NET 11 SDK for a simulator that runs on .NET 10. That rule is more restrictive than the behaviour of MSBuildWorkspace itself, which evaluates projects in a separate build host process launched with `--roll-forward LatestMajor` and then relaunched from the `dotnet` executable of the selected MSBuild.

For Metalama.Framework.Workspaces, Metalama.LinqPad and Metalama.Tool, the same rule selects the .NET 11 SDK only when the hosting process runs on .NET 11. A user application that targets net11.0 receives the net10.0 asset of the package and runs on the .NET 11 runtime, so it reaches the .NET 11 SDK. The tools do not reach it as easily: Metalama.Tool targets net10.0 with `RollForward=Major`, and that policy rolls forward to a higher major version only when no runtime of the requested major version is installed. On a machine that has both the .NET 10 and the .NET 11 runtimes, Metalama.Tool runs on .NET 10 and its MSBuildInitializer never selects the .NET 11 SDK.
corrections.proposed_change:
Give Metalama.DesignTime.HostSimulator a net11.0 target and make `_simulatorTargetFramework` follow the .NET SDK that the build uses, rather than a constant, then add a DesignTimeStandalone scenario containing a net11.0 project. The scenario also requires the build SDK pinned in eng/src/Program.cs to be a .NET 11 SDK, because a .NET 10 SDK rejects a net11.0 project before restore. `RollForward=Major` on a single net10.0 simulator target is not a sufficient alternative, because that policy keeps the process on .NET 10 whenever a .NET 10 runtime is installed; `LatestMajor` would be required, and it would still have to be reconciled with the SDK selection rule.

Separately, re-examine the selection rule `sdk.Version.Major <= Environment.Version.Major` in MSBuildEnvironment.cs:50 and MSBuildInitializer.cs:84 for Metalama.Tool and Metalama.LinqPad. It makes the tool refuse the .NET 11 SDK whenever the tool process happens to run on .NET 10, which is the ordinary case for a net10.0 application with `RollForward=Major`. Roslyn does not impose that restriction on itself: it delegates project evaluation to an out-of-process build host that rolls forward to the latest major runtime. Whether the in-process MSBuildLocator registration constrains that build host through the inherited MSBUILD_EXE_PATH, MSBuildExtensionsPath and MSBuildSDKsPath variables has to be measured before the rule is relaxed. Keeping Metalama.Framework.Workspaces at net10.0 is correct and should be left unchanged.
corrections.consequence_class: Coverage gap for design-time scenarios on net11.0, plus a possible functional limitation of Metalama.Tool and Metalama.LinqPad on net11.0 projects when the tool process runs on the .NET 10 runtime.
corrections.size: M

notes:
The finding survives, so the verdict is "corrected" rather than "refuted": every in-repo citation is accurate, the package-asset premise is true, and the conclusion that no design-time scenario can contain a net11.0 project is true. Four corrections are needed.

First, a version label. The finding names "Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspaces.MSBuild 5.10". No stable package with that number exists; the stable is 5.9.0 and the version expected for the 2027.0 baseline is 5.12. The asset claim is nevertheless true of 5.9.0, of the consumed prerelease 5.10.0-1.26365.3, and of dotnet/roslyn main, so the conclusion drawn from it stands and even strengthens: the workspaces project cannot move to net11.0 by raising the Roslyn version.

Second, the stated cause of the coverage gap is incomplete. The finding derives the absence of net11.0 design-time scenarios from the runtime of the simulator process. The controlling constraint is the .NET SDK version pinned for the build: a .NET 10 SDK raises UnsupportedTargetFrameworkVersion for a net11.0 project before restore, so the scenario cannot even be restored. The proposed change must therefore include moving the pinned build SDK, not only the simulator target framework.

Third, `RollForward=Major` does not put the tools on the .NET 11 runtime on a machine that has a .NET 10 runtime. This is the opposite of what the finding states, and it makes the consequence larger rather than smaller: Metalama.Tool would refuse the .NET 11 SDK in the ordinary configuration. It also invalidates the alternative suggested at the end of the proposed change, which offered `RollForward=Major` on the simulator as a single-target option.

Fourth, the premise that a host process on .NET 10 can never reach the MSBuild of the .NET 11 SDK is true of in-process MSBuild loading but not of MSBuildWorkspace as a whole, which evaluates projects in a build host process that rolls forward to the latest major runtime and relaunches under the `dotnet` executable of the selected MSBuild. Metalama's own selection rule is stricter than Roslyn's. Whether that strictness is required is a question about the interaction between MSBuildLocator's process-wide environment variables and the build host, and it should be measured in the code rather than assumed. This does not change the finding's verdict; it adds an item to verify before the rule is relaxed.

One premise class named in the task does not appear in this finding: UT-8 makes no statement about C# 15 semantics, the csharplang proposals, or the Roslyn public API surface, so the csharplang proposals under csharp-15.0 were not consulted.

evidence:
UT-13 makes no claim about C# 15 semantics, about a csharplang proposal, about the Roslyn public API or about the Roslyn version timeline, so those premise families are inapplicable to it. Its only external premise family is the .NET SDK, and two statements there need correction.

1. "its MSBuild, whose version is unknown offline". This is now known. The dotnet/sdk `main` branch is the .NET 11 SDK line: `eng/Versions.props` lines 6-12 read `VersionMajor` 11, `VersionMinor` 0, `VersionSDKMinor` 1, `PreReleaseVersionLabel` rc, giving 11.0.1xx. Its `eng/Version.Details.xml` line 31 pins `Dependency Name="Microsoft.Build" Version="18.12.0-1.26452.110"` (with `Microsoft.Build.Localization` and `Microsoft.Build.TaskAuthoring.Analyzer` at the same version, lines 35 and 39). The .NET 11 SDK therefore carries MSBuild 18.12, which is above the pinned 18.0.2. The same file, line 87, pins `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspaces.MSBuild` at `5.12.0-1.26452.110`, which independently corroborates the FACTS addendum statement that the November 2026 baseline carries Roslyn 5.12 and not 5.10 or 5.11 (FACTS.md lines 48-49).

2. "`Microsoft.Build` keeps a frozen assembly version (`Directory.Packages.md:309`)". The cited line asserts the frozen assembly version for the 17.x line only: "Some .NET libraries keep AsmVer frozen across NuGet patches (e.g., `Microsoft.Build` 17.x all expose AsmVer 15.1.0.0)". I measured the 18.x line directly. The packages `Microsoft.Build` 17.14.28, 18.0.2 and 18.9.6 were downloaded from nuget.org and their CLI metadata Assembly table was read: every asset, `lib/net472` and `lib/net10.0` (and `lib/net9.0` for 17.14.28), declares AssemblyVersion 15.1.0.0. `Microsoft.Build.Framework` 18.0.2 and 18.9.6, `lib/net10.0`, likewise declare 15.1.0.0. The premise therefore holds through the whole 18.x line, not only 17.x, and the finding's binding argument stands on a measured fact rather than on an extrapolation from the cited line.

3. The residual risk the finding names, "only API removals would break", was tested as far as the public feed allows. The public type and member sets of the `Microsoft.Build` namespace were extracted from `lib/net10.0/Microsoft.Build.dll` in 18.0.2 and 18.9.6: 2237 entries against 2270, with zero entries present in 18.0.2 and absent from 18.9.6. `Microsoft.Build.Framework` gives 798 against 843, again with zero removals. No public API of the 18.0.2 surface has been removed anywhere in the published 18.x line. The exact SDK build cannot be checked, because the nuget.org flat-container index of `Microsoft.Build` lists 18.0.2, 18.3.3, 18.4.0, 18.6.3, 18.7.1, 18.8.2 and 18.9.6 and no 18.10, 18.11 or 18.12.

4. The surface Metalama compiles against is small and long-standing: `Microsoft.Build.Evaluation.ProjectCollection` (constructor, `RegisterLogger`, `LoadProject`) at Metalama.Framework/src/Metalama.Framework.Workspaces/Workspace.cs:344-386, `Microsoft.Build.Evaluation.Project.GetProperty`, `ExpandString` and `Properties` at Metalama.Framework/src/Metalama.Framework.Workspaces/WorkspaceProjectOptions.cs:71-85, and `Microsoft.Build.Framework.ILogger`, `IEventSource`, `BuildMessageEventArgs`, `BuildWarningEventArgs`, `BuildErrorEventArgs`, `MessageImportance` and `LoggerVerbosity` at Metalama.Framework/src/Metalama.Framework.Workspaces/MSBuildLogger.cs:5-51. None of these members appears in the removal set above.

5. The policy premise, that the pin follows the lowest host and that the lowest host stays the .NET 10 SDK, is confirmed by Metalama.Framework/docs/platform-support.md:196-197, "The floor is the .NET 10 SDK. The .NET 11 SDK, released in November 2026, is also in the set", and by Directory.Packages.props:35-50 and Directory.Packages.md:63-69. Adding `net11.0` as a user target framework does not move the host floor, so the pin of 18.0.2 (Directory.Packages.props:50), which is the lowest 18.0 published on nuget.org, stays correct.

The finding survives all of this: the consequence class "No impact expected" is unchanged, and the two corrections make it stronger rather than weaker.

notes:
Method. The three `Microsoft.Build` packages and the two `Microsoft.Build.Framework` packages were downloaded from the nuget.org flat container into /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Metalama/ccf204f4-b0b3-5fe6-a8de-fe20f6791d2c/scratchpad/msb. Assembly versions and the public type, method and field sets were read from the CLI metadata tables with the `dnfile` Python package; the member sets were restricted to types whose namespace begins with `Microsoft.Build.`, because the unrestricted set also contains public members nested inside internal types, which are not part of the public surface. The `dotnet/sdk` files were fetched from `raw.githubusercontent.com`. No file in /home/user/Metalama or /home/user/metalama.premium was modified, and nothing was built.

Two observations outside the premise families I was asked to check, offered so that the theme owner can decide whether they belong elsewhere.

First, the finding's parenthetical "(UT-8)" for the selected SDK is supported by the local code, not only by UT-8. `Metalama.Framework/src/Metalama.Framework.Workspaces/MSBuildInitializer.cs` does not use the SDK discovery of `Microsoft.Build.Locator`. It runs `dotnet --list-sdks`, filters to SDKs whose major version is at most `Environment.Version.Major`, takes the highest, and passes the result to `MSBuildLocator.RegisterInstance`. On a .NET 10 process an installed 11.x SDK is therefore excluded, and on a .NET 11 process it is selected. This is a code-lens matter and I did not verify it beyond reading the file.

Second, a residual risk that UT-13 does not name. `MSBuildInitializer.cs` builds its `VisualStudioInstance` by reflecting on a non-public constructor with the signature `(string, string, Version, DiscoveryType)` and throws `AssertionFailedException` when it is absent. `Microsoft.Build.Locator` is pinned at 1.7.8 (`Directory.Packages.props:151`), so the reflection is stable today, but `dotnet/sdk` `main` uses `Microsoft.Build.Locator` 1.10.2 (`eng/Versions.props` line 134) and nuget.org publishes up to 1.11.2. Any future bump of that pin, whether or not it is motivated by .NET 11, has to re-verify that constructor. Neither BaseCodeHasher nor SafeSyntaxWalker overrides DefaultVisit (grep over both directories returns only PartialTypesVisitor.cs:18 and PartialTypesHasher.cs:21), so CSharpSyntaxWalker.DefaultVisit runs for a union declaration and, at depth Node, visits child nodes only. corrections.what_happens_today: `RunTimeCodeHasher` and `CompileTimeCodeHasher` are generated with one `Visit<Node>` override per grammar node (`Generator.cs:615-708`), and the generator strips every node and field that carries `ExperimentalUrl` (`TreeReader.cs:37` and `TreeReader.cs:57`). Two consequences follow. First, `UnionDeclarationSyntax` has no override, so `CSharpSyntaxWalker.DefaultVisit` runs; the walker is constructed with `SyntaxWalkerDepth.Node` (`SafeSyntaxWalker.cs:39`, reached because `BaseCodeHasher.cs:26` calls no base overload), which visits child nodes and skips tokens. The union identifier, its modifiers and the `union` keyword are tokens of that node and contribute nothing to the hash, while the node-typed fields that the grammar declares at `Syntax-5.10.0.xml:1954` still do: the attribute lists, the type parameter list, the parameter list, the base list, the constraint clauses and the members. The grammar declares no separate case-type field; the cases are members. Second, the generated `VisitBreakStatement` and `VisitContinueStatement` hash only the attribute lists, the keyword and the semicolon, because the `Name` field was removed before generation, so the label of a labeled `break` or `continue` is never hashed even by `CompileTimeCodeHasher`, which otherwise hashes bodies. `DiffStrategy.IsDifferent` treats an equal hash as no change (lines 80-85) and `CompilationChanges.cs:206-226` records a `SyntaxTreeChange` only when it returns true, so the pipeline is not re-run. Observable effects, which become reachable only once C# 15 is reachable in a Metalama project (today `Metalama.Framework.targets` rewrites an unrecognised `LangVersion` and `VerifyLanguageVersion` rejects preview unless preview features are allowed): renaming a union, or adding `partial` to it in response to LAMA0048, in a file with no other change does not trigger re-analysis, so the stale result and the stale LAMA0048 persist until an unrelated edit; changing the target label of `break` or `continue` inside a template does not rebuild the compile-time project, so the template keeps its previous behaviour at design time. Separately, `PartialTypesVisitor` and `PartialTypesHasher` override only class, struct and record, so a partial union is never listed in `SyntaxTreeVersion.PartialTypes` and the partial-type invalidation of `SyntaxTreeChange.cs:111` and `DiffStrategy.cs:97-150` does not cover unions, whereas `DependencyCollector.cs:63-64` does register unions because it tests `BaseTypeDeclarationSyntax`. That omission is not specific to unions: `VisitInterfaceDeclaration` is not overridden either, so a partial interface is already treated the same way today. The whole mechanism is confined to `Metalama.Framework.DesignTime`, so a batch compilation is not affected.
corrections.proposed_change: As part of the update to the next stable Roslyn, which is 5.12 and not 5.10, add the stable grammar as a new file `eng/src/GenerateMetaSyntaxRewriter/Syntax-5.12.0.xml` and list it in `GenerateMetaSyntaxRewriter.cs`, following `updating-roslyn.md:12-13`, which explicitly forbids overwriting or renaming the previous version's file. Then regenerate: the union node and the break and continue `Name` field lose their `ExperimentalUrl` when the features ship in C# 15, so the generator will emit the missing overrides and hash the missing field. Add `VisitUnionDeclaration` overrides to `PartialTypesVisitor` and `PartialTypesHasher`, and decide at the same time whether `VisitInterfaceDeclaration` should be added as well, because a partial interface has the same gap today. These two classes are `CSharpSyntaxVisitor<T>` and are compiled for both variants, and `UnionDeclarationSyntax` does not exist in the Roslyn 5.0.0 assemblies (`Syntax-5.0.0.xml` declares it nowhere), so the overrides must be guarded. No new file and no policy exception are required: `eng/RoslynVersions/Roslyn.5.10.0.props` already defines `ROSLYN_5_10_0_OR_GREATER` for the latest variant, `Latest.props` imports it, and `Metalama.Framework.DesignTime.csproj:3` imports `Latest.props`, so a `#if` guard in the shared source is available; `updating-roslyn.md:36` restricts adding a new constant, not using the existing one. Add a `DiffStrategy` unit test that renames a union and changes a `break` label and asserts that the hash changes. The test must parse with an explicit `CSharpParseOptions`, because the existing tests in `CompilationChangesTests.IsDifferent.cs` use the default options; and it cannot be gated on `LanguageVersionFacts.TryParse("15.0")`, because `LanguageVersion.CSharp15` does not exist in the Roslyn build that is consumed today, so such a test would be skipped unconditionally. Gate it on the variant constant instead, and use `LanguageVersion.Preview` until the move to 5.12.

notes:
The central claim holds in the code. The generator strips the experimental union node and the experimental `Name` field of `break` and `continue` before emitting the hashers, the hashers walk at `SyntaxWalkerDepth.Node` and therefore skip the tokens of a node that has no override, and an equal hash produces no `SyntaxTreeChange` at all. Nothing on that path throws or reports a diagnostic, so `Silent wrong output` is the right consequence class; it should be read as design-time staleness only, because `DiffStrategy` exists only in `Metalama.Framework.DesignTime` and a batch compilation does not use it.

Four details are wrong and are corrected above.

First, the version. The title and the proposed change name a stable Roslyn 5.10. Per the verified addendum the next stable Roslyn is 5.12, and the consumed `5.10.0-1.26365.3` is a main build with no stable counterpart. The title should read "until the grammar is refreshed from the stable Roslyn 5.12"; the `corrections` schema has no title field, so I record it here.

Second, the procedure. The proposal says to copy the stable grammar over `Syntax-5.10.0.xml`. `Metalama.Framework/docs/updating-roslyn.md:12` requires a new file named after the new version and says in terms "Do not rename the previous version's file instead", and `:13` requires the new file to be listed in `GenerateMetaSyntaxRewriter.cs`.

Third, the variant mechanism. The proposal asserts that a guarded override needs either a kind-testing `DefaultVisit` or a file compiled for one variant only, "which is a policy exception to record". That is not so. `eng/RoslynVersions/Roslyn.5.10.0.props` already defines `ROSLYN_5_10_0_OR_GREATER`, `Latest.props` imports it and `Metalama.Framework.DesignTime.csproj:3` imports `Latest.props`, so a preprocessor guard in the shared source is available today; `updating-roslyn.md:36` restricts only the addition of a new constant. The two classes are also `CSharpSyntaxVisitor<T>`, not walkers, so the phrase "a walker override cannot be resolved by name" describes them inaccurately, although the underlying constraint (the type does not exist in Roslyn 5.0.0, as `Syntax-5.0.0.xml` confirms) is real.

Fourth, the proposed test. It is to be skipped when `LanguageVersionFacts.TryParse("15.0")` fails. `LanguageVersion.CSharp15` is absent from every Roslyn build that Metalama consumes today, so that gate would skip the test unconditionally and it would never run, not even in the latest variant. The variant constant is the correct gate, with `LanguageVersion.Preview` as the parse option until the move to 5.12.

Two smaller inaccuracies are folded into the corrected `what_happens_today`. `UnionDeclarationSyntax` has no case-type field, so "the case types ... still do" should read as the node-typed fields the grammar actually declares. And the partial-type gap is not specific to unions: `VisitInterfaceDeclaration` is overridden in neither `PartialTypesVisitor` nor `PartialTypesHasher`, so a partial interface is already invisible to the partial-type invalidation while `DependencyCollector` registers it. Adding only the union override would leave that older inconsistency in place, which is worth deciding deliberately rather than by omission.

One scope caveat that the finding does not state: a union declaration cannot appear in a Metalama-supported project today, because `Metalama.Framework.targets` rewrites an unrecognised `LangVersion` and `VerifyLanguageVersion` rejects preview unless preview features are allowed. The defect is therefore latent and becomes observable only when C# 15 becomes reachable, which is consistent with the forward-looking framing of the finding but should be said explicitly.

The Roslyn parser produces an UnsafeExpressionSyntax for any text of the form unsafe(e) in expression position, whatever the language version (LanguageParser.cs:11993-11994 and :12715-12722 on dotnet/roslyn main); the language version is checked only when the expression is bound (Binder_Expressions.cs:7628). A project at C# 14, which VerifyLanguageVersion accepts, therefore already presents the node to the annotator, together with the compiler error ERR_FeatureInPreview and, when AllowUnsafeBlocks is off, ERR_IllegalUnsafe. The preview flag is not a precondition of the defect; it only decides whether the compile-time pipeline runs at all in a project that sets LangVersion to preview, and the design-time pipeline performs no such check (CompileTimeAspectPipeline.cs:64-65). Second, the disjunction "If Roslyn rejects the preview expression there ... If Roslyn accepts it" can be resolved. The compile-time compilation is created with a language version that is the minimum of the software development kit version and the project version and is therefore never Preview (LanguageVersionProvider.cs:45-72, CompileTimeCompilationBuilder.cs:279), and its CSharpCompilationOptions do not set AllowUnsafe (CompileTimeCompilationBuilder.cs:448). Roslyn consequently reports both ERR_FeatureInPreview and ERR_IllegalUnsafe on the generated compile-time file. Only the first branch occurs; the silent branch does not occur through this path. Add for accuracy that unsafe(e) is not merely a wrapper that evaluates to e: it establishes an unsafe context for the enclosed expression (proposals/unsafe-evolution.md:408-412), so removing it from the generated run-time code is a semantic change even when the value is unchanged.
corrections.consequence_class: A diagnostic reported in the wrong place: the compile-time compilation reports the C# errors ERR_FeatureInPreview and ERR_IllegalUnsafe on the generated compile-time file instead of the template reporting LAMA0101 on the unsafe expression. The silent-wrong-output alternative does not arise, because the compile-time compilation is never at the preview language version and never allows unsafe code.

A name-free guard driven by the generator is therefore still required for this node after the move to 5.12, and it is required for this node alone. Two adjustments. First, the test does not need @AllowPreviewLanguageFeatures to exercise the guard, because the node parses at C# 14; a preview test remains useful, but a C# 14 test proves the guard as well. Second, the open question about BreakStatementSyntax.Name is answered differently than it assumes: on main the Name field is no longer experimental (Syntax.xml:2503, PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt:21 and :24), so the generator will emit code for it once the grammar is refreshed, and the ExperimentalKindNames mechanism does not apply to it in any case, because labeled break and continue introduce no new SyntaxKind. The only obstacle to naming the property is that Roslyn 5.0.0 does not have it and production source carries no conditional compilation, which is a separate design constraint from experimentality.

notes:
The finding survives. Its central external premises are true: the unsafe expression is a real new node in the Roslyn versions Metalama consumes and in the expected target version 5.12; it is a preview feature and not part of C# 15, so it is out of scope of the C# 15 work but reachable by users; the node type cannot be named from shared production source, both because Roslyn 5.0.0 does not define it and because it remains experimental on main, unlike the union, with-element and labeled-break API whose experimental markers were removed by the C# 15 commit of 2026-08-11.

Two premises are wrong and are corrected above. The first is the claim that the expression is parseable only under preview. Roslyn parses it unconditionally and reports the feature error during binding, so the annotator sees the node in an ordinary C# 14 project and the missing LAMA0101 is not conditional on MetalamaAllowPreviewLanguageFeatures. This widens rather than narrows the finding. The second is the unresolved disjunction about the compile-time compilation. The compile-time compilation is fixed at a non-preview language version and does not allow unsafe code, so Roslyn always rejects the emitted unsafe expression and the outcome is always the misplaced diagnostic. The consequence class should be narrowed accordingly, and the confidence of that part can move from plausible to verified.

One accuracy point on the description of the semantics: the proposal defines the type and value of unsafe(e) as those of e, but the construct also establishes an unsafe context that does not extend beyond the closing parenthesis. Dropping the wrapper is therefore not a value-preserving simplification in general; in generated run-time code it can turn a legal expression into one that requires an unsafe context.

Two minor inaccuracies in the supporting report, neither of which affects the finding: the comment "keep this in preview until C# 16" quoted by the Roslyn API delta report is not present in MessageID.cs on main, although the preview classification it supports is correct; and the delta report describes BreakStatementSyntax.Name as experimental, which is true of the consumed 5.10 preview and of 5.9.0 but false of main.

Priority remark, offered as context and not as a correction: exercising this path requires a user project that both enables AllowUnsafeBlocks and writes an unsafe expression in a template, and the preview status of the feature means it cannot appear in a project that pins a released language version without also producing a compiler error. The guard is cheap, but the scenario is narrow.

evidence: Central claim confirmed. ProduceCompileTimeCodeRewriter overrides only VisitClassDeclaration, VisitStructDeclaration, VisitInterfaceDeclaration, VisitRecordDeclaration, VisitEnumDeclaration and VisitDelegateDeclaration (CompileTimeCompilationBuilder.ProduceCompileTimeCodeRewriter.cs:204-234); there is no VisitUnionDeclaration or VisitExtensionBlockDeclaration anywhere in the engine (grep over Metalama.Framework/src returns only Linking/LinkerLinkingStep.LinkingRewriter.cs:79 and Linking/LinkerInjectionStep.Rewriter.cs:324 for extension blocks, nothing for unions). In TransformCompileTimeType the nested-type case lists ClassDeclaration, StructDeclaration, InterfaceDeclaration, RecordDeclaration and RecordStructDeclaration (:540-544) and the default case calls this.Visit(member) (:557-558); SafeSyntaxRewriter.Visit forwards to CSharpSyntaxRewriter.Visit (Metalama.Framework.Sdk/Utilities/Roslyn/SafeSyntaxRewriter.cs:44-63), so a union is copied with its members, subject only to the VisitAttributeList (:147), VisitIdentifierName (:1718), VisitToken (:1630) and VisitTrivia (:1778) overrides; no VisitMethodDeclaration override exists, so templates in the union are not transformed and AddToManifestIfNecessary (:380) is never called for them. In PopulateNestedCompileTimeTypes (:254-378) the ClassDeclaration case is :271-354, the struct/interface/record/record struct/enum/delegate case is :356-371, and the default case (:373-376) ignores any other member, so a compile-time union nested in a run-time type is dropped without diagnostic. TemplateAnnotator.cs:743-754 overrides class, struct, record, delegate and enum (no interface) and VisitTypeDeclaration :756-775 returns run-time types without descent; TemplatingCodeValidator.Visitor.cs:299-329 overrides class, struct, record and interface. Pinned behaviour: Tests/Fabrics/ErrorNestedTypeNotFabric.cs and .t.cs (LAMA0231 for enum, interface, struct, delegate, record, class; LAMA0229 for a [RunTimeOrCompileTime] nested class). Corrections are supported by: CompileTimeCompilationBuilder.cs:599-647 (emit failure reports CannotEmitCompileTimeAssembly plus every Roslyn error), ProduceCompileTimeCodeRewriter.cs:463-495 (run-time compilation errors inside a compile-time type are reported and set Success=false), TemplateProjectManifest.cs:27-30 and :36-60 (scope lookup inherits the last scope recorded on a containing symbol), Syntax-5.10.0.xml:2083 and Syntax-5.0.0.xml:2036 (ExtensionBlockDeclarationSyntax derives from TypeDeclarationSyntax), Directory.Build.props:9 (NoWarn contains only IDE0032 and IDE0031), Metalama.Testing.AspectTesting/TestOptions.cs:681-690 (an unparseable integer @LanguageVersion skips the test), FACTS.md:27 and :53-56 (experimental markers, absence of CSharp15 in consumed builds).

corrections.what_happens_today: The description holds for the Roslyn 5.10 variant with the following precisions. (1) The union copied through the default case (:557-558) is not entirely verbatim: the base rewriter descends into it, so the VisitAttributeList (:147), VisitIdentifierName (:1718), VisitToken (:1630) and VisitTrivia (:1778) overrides still apply to its content; what is missing is the per-member transformation (TransformMethodDeclaration and the other Transform* methods, :515-538) and the manifest registration (:380). (2) The missing manifest entry is only partly silent: TemplateProjectManifest.GetNodeInfo (TemplateProjectManifest.cs:36-60) inherits the last scope recorded on a containing symbol, so a referencing project still classifies the nested union with the scope of its containing compile-time type; what is lost is the TemplateInfo of any template declared inside the union. (3) The annotator and the validator do not hold kind lists; they hold per-kind overrides. The annotator overrides class, struct, record, delegate and enum and has no VisitInterfaceDeclaration (TemplateAnnotator.cs:743-754); the validator overrides class, struct, record and interface (TemplatingCodeValidator.Visitor.cs:299-329). For a union, the base walker descends into the members, and each member still obtains its own scope through WithDeclaration (:828-846) or VisitMemberDeclaration (TemplateAnnotator.cs:1850-1895); the union node itself receives no scope annotation and VerifyTypeDeclaration (:332) is not run on it. (4) ExtensionBlockDeclarationSyntax, which also derives from TypeDeclarationSyntax (Syntax-5.0.0.xml:2036), already takes the same default path in all three visitors today; the union is the second node kind on this path, not the first. (5) In the Roslyn 5.0 variant the parser does not produce a union node, so the scenario does not arise there; the errors of the run-time compilation are reported by TransformCompileTimeType (:463-495).
corrections.consequence_class: Depends on the compile-time language version. As long as the compile-time compilation is created with C# 14 (CompileTimeCompilationBuilder.cs:349-354, FACTS.md:16-17) and the consumed Roslyn gates unions on LanguageVersion.Preview (FACTS.md:54), a copied union fails the compile-time emit, and CannotEmitCompileTimeAssembly plus every Roslyn error are reported (CompileTimeCompilationBuilder.cs:599-647): diagnostic reported, not silent. The silent wrong output (untransformed templates inside the union, missing TemplateInfo entries, dropped nested compile-time union in a run-time type) appears only once TP-8 raises the compile-time language version so that the union compiles. The dropped union in a run-time type is silent in either state; a compile-time reference to it then fails in the compile-time compilation with reported errors.
corrections.proposed_change: After regeneration (which, per FACTS.md:27 and :55, requires the stable Roslyn 5.12 where the experimental markers are removed), add SyntaxKind.UnionDeclaration to the two kind lists of ProduceCompileTimeCodeRewriter (:356-357 and :540-541) and add a VisitUnionDeclaration override beside VisitRecordDeclaration in ProduceCompileTimeCodeRewriter (:210), TemplateAnnotator (:748) and TemplatingCodeValidator.Visitor (:313). Two constraints apply. First, the Roslyn 5.0 variant cannot name UnionDeclarationSyntax or SyntaxKind.UnionDeclaration, and the consumed 5.10 preview marks both with RSEXPERIMENTAL006 while no NoWarn covers it (Directory.Build.props:9), so the overrides need either the ROSLYN_5_10_0_OR_GREATER (later 5_12_0) guard or the move to the stable Roslyn; the kind lists can instead be replaced by a `member is TypeDeclarationSyntax` pattern that needs no guard. Second, that pattern also captures ExtensionBlockDeclarationSyntax, which derives from TypeDeclarationSyntax in both variants (Syntax-5.0.0.xml:2036, Syntax-5.10.0.xml:2083) and currently takes the default path in all three visitors; the pattern must exclude extension blocks (`member is TypeDeclarationSyntax and not ExtensionBlockDeclarationSyntax`) or handle them deliberately, otherwise it changes the handling of C# 14 extension members in compile-time types and, in PopulateNestedCompileTimeTypes, starts reporting LAMA0231 on extension blocks of run-time types. Add the aspect tests Tests/Aspects/CSharp15/Unions/Union_NestedInAspect.cs and Union_NestedInRunTimeType.cs with // @LanguageVersion(15.0); TestOptions.cs:681-690 skips such a test on any Roslyn that cannot parse 15.0, and the test also depends on TP-8 adding CSharp15 to SupportedCSharpVersions.All (FACTS.md:21). Extend Tests/Fabrics/ErrorNestedTypeNotFabric.cs with a [CompileTime] union under the same guard, so that the run-time-type case is pinned as LAMA0231 like structs.
corrections.size: S after regeneration.

notes: The open question (whether a union in a run-time type must be un-nested like a TypeFabric) is answered by the existing test: every non-class nested compile-time type is reported as LAMA0231 (ErrorNestedTypeNotFabric.t.cs), and a union cannot inherit TypeFabric, so reporting LAMA0231 through the :356-371 case is the consistent choice. The SourceNamedTypeImpl.TypeKind claim (:69-78) is outside this theme and was not refuted: the method throws for any Roslyn TypeKind outside the six listed, and ExtensionBlockImpl.cs:30 shows that the extension case is handled by an override rather than by SourceNamedTypeImpl; whether union symbols report TypeKind.Class is a Roslyn semantic that this session cannot verify (Metalama.Compiler and the Roslyn sources are not available). An MSBuild task assembly is not started by the host. The documentation sentence it cites conflates the two cases as well, because it justifies the tasks with the roll-forward policy of the compiler.

notes:
The finding survives. Every load-bearing external premise is true: the union declaration is a `TypeDeclarationSyntax` whose kind is absent from Metalama's kind list, `partial` is a legal union modifier, a union body may carry members, and a union symbol arrives as an ordinary named type of `TypeKind.Struct`. Four corrections are needed.

First, version naming. The finding speaks of "Roslyn 5.10" and of C# 15 as if both were available. Per the addendum of FACTS.md, no stable 5.10 exists, the target stable is 5.12, and in the consumed 5.10.0-1.26365.3 preview `LanguageVersion.CSharp15` does not exist. Because the parser recognises `union` only when the unions feature is enabled (LanguageParser.cs:1678-1690), the defect is reachable today only under LangVersion preview, and becomes a normal scenario after the move to Roslyn 5.12.

Second, the proposed change is incomplete and therefore under-sized. Correcting only the kind test makes `IsPartial` true and lets `DesignTimeSyntaxTreeGenerator` proceed, but that generator selects the declaration form from Metalama's `TypeKind`, where a union is a struct, so the generated file would say `partial struct U { ... }` and the compilation would fail with CS0261. Roslyn's own test `UnionDeclaration_05` demonstrates exactly this pairing. The generated part must be `partial union U { ... }` with no case-type list, because only one part may carry the list (CS8863) and at least one must (CS9370). Emitting it requires `SyntaxFactory.UnionDeclaration`, which cannot be named in source that also compiles against Roslyn 5.0, so the fix needs a variant-scoped file or generated text rather than a single shared expression. I raised the size to L for that reason.

Third, the stated rationale for `Enum.TryParse` is wrong although the technique is right. `SyntaxKind.UnionDeclaration` is 9082 in the 5.10 window, in the 5.11 window and on main, so the value has not moved. The real reasons are that the constant is absent from Roslyn 5.0 and that naming it against 5.9 or 5.10 raises the experimental-API diagnostic, which the compiler reports as an error by default.

Fourth, a test-plan qualification. A union body rejects instance fields, auto-properties, field-like events (CS9373) and a public single-parameter constructor (CS9374), so an aspect test must introduce a method or another permitted member; an introduced auto-property or field would fail for a reason unrelated to the defect.

Open questions of the finding: the first is answered for main, where `UnionDeclarationSyntax` still derives from `TypeDeclarationSyntax` and no longer carries `ExperimentalUrl`; it remains unverifiable for a stable package, since none exists. The second is confirmed as a code-model theme: `ITypeSymbol.IsUnion` exists on main and in the consumed build (experimental there), while `ITypeSymbol.UnionCaseTypes` was added after the consumed build and is available only from 5.11 onward.

Not verified here: the behaviour of the actual package 5.10.0-1.26365.3, which the API delta report could not read directly; the Roslyn version that the .NET 11 general availability software development kit will carry; and whether Metalama.Compiler, which is not cloned, can move to Roslyn 5.12.
